resources.string: Sleevesight reads what your music player is playing, looks it up in the sources you switch on, and has the AI service you choose write about it. Before you start, here is what it reads, and what leaves your phone.

Sleevesight needs notification access, which is how Android lets an app read what a player is playing. It checks which players report music (a track with a title and an artist), to list them in its settings by name, and keeps or sends nothing of the players you do not follow. From the players you follow (Spotify by default), it reads which player it is; the title, artists, album, length and cover; whether it is playing, and how far into the track; and the queue of tracks up next, with its name. It ignores the notifications themselves, never reads calls from the phone app or sessions Android marks as voice calls, and never touches the audio.
What leaves the phone, and to whom

To the sources you switch on, such as MusicBrainz and Wikipedia (with Wikidata): the title and artists of the playing track, cleaned of tags such as “2006 Remaster”. Wikidata gets only identifiers. For the genre labels, Last.fm also gets the album name, the only source that does. While “Prepare the next track” is set to “Evidence”, as it is by default, the title and artists of the next track in the player’s queue also go to MusicBrainz, if switched on.

To the AI service you choose: the title, artists and album, and what the sources found. This is for the playing track only: the next one in the queue is looked up ahead, but no insight is written for it until it plays.
Your API keys: each only to the service it belongs to, with each request to it.
To the server a cover’s web address names, when a player gives the cover only as a web address: a request for that image. The address itself may identify the album or episode.
Each of these services also sees your phone’s IP address, as every service you connect to does.

Nothing else leaves the phone, unless you export the diagnostics to a file yourself. The length and cover of each track, the list of tracks played, and the record of track changes used to tell your skips from natural ends stay on it, and are left out of Android’s backup. Your API keys are stored encrypted and never logged.
No accounts of our own, no telemetry, no crash reporting of our own, no analytics, no ads.
The privacy policy says more, with where Sleevesight stands under the GDPR and the EU AI Act:

Keep Sources as you left them

Off: the sources under each new track’s insight start folded. On: they stay folded, or unfolded, as you left them on the track before; shown past their first 8 entries but not in full, they come back at their first 8.
Off: lookups and insights only while Sleevesight is on screen. On: insights written automatically are paid calls on your key, made while Sleevesight is not on screen.
How long each source’s findings are kept
Keep what sources said about each artist

Off: nothing MusicBrainz, Wikipedia or Last.fm say about an artist is kept, so each track’s artists are looked up again, and their names go to the sources you switch on with every track. Of a track’s findings, only the web search’s findings (pages about the recording, which may name or describe its artists) and those of a lookup that found no artist to look up are kept, so a track played before is looked up again at MusicBrainz (its match held in memory for half an hour only), Wikipedia and Last.fm, unless it has no credited artist, and lookups are slower and more requests go out. On: what they say about each artist you play stays on this phone for as long as its sources’ findings, so fewer requests leave it; each track’s own lookups still send its artists’ names. Turning this off deletes what was kept.

resources.string: Sleevesight is free software, under the GNU General Public License, version 3. What it shows comes from these sources, its text is set in this font, and its icons come from this set, each under its own terms.
Recordings, releases, artists, credits and dates, from MusicBrainz.
Genre labels, from the artists’ tags by MusicBrainz contributors. Used for labels only, never sent to the AI service.
Sentences from articles, by Wikipedia contributors.
Facts on songs and artists, from Wikidata.
Artist bios by Last.fm users, under CC BY-SA; listeners, tags, genre labels and similar artists under Last.fm’s API terms.
Web search results, under Exa’s terms of service.
The app’s font, Roboto 3.016, from github.com/googlefonts/roboto-3-classic. Copyright 2011 The Roboto Project Authors.
The icons in the app, such as the cogwheel, from Material Symbols by Google.
